newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - No urgent need for UK tax rises, study shows.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - No urgent need for UK tax rises, study shows.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government faces no pressing need to raise taxes in its first budget because public finances are in fairly healthy shape, two leading financial institutions said on Tuesday.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) and investment bank Goldman Sachs International said tax revenue was set to rise as a result of steady economic growth, even if the government did nothing.

In their "Green Budget," in which they provide analysis and advice on the forthcoming budget, they said higher interest rates would be a more appropriate way of reining in rampant consumer spending to stop inflation getting out of control.
"We do not actually think that there is a major problem with the budget deficit at the moment," Goldman Sachs chief international economist Gavyn Davies said.
Budget plans which Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown inherited from the ousted Conservatives already contained a significant fiscal tightening.
"We are tightening by about one percent of GDP per year at the moment," Davies told a presentation on the Green Budget. "There is quite a lot of fiscal restraint in the pipeline."

The views set out in the Green Budget are at odds with much of the prevailing wisdom in the City of London. Many economists argue that the tax burden must be increased to dampen demand and reduce upward pressure on interest rates.
No date has yet been set for Brown's first budget but it is expected by early July.

The Bank of England, newly empowered by Brown to set interest rates, has warned that official rates will have to rise from the present 6.25 percent to prevent strong consumer spending from leading to higher inflation.
David Walton, director of UK economic research at Goldman Sachs, said the best way historically to dent consumer confidence was through higher interest rates.
"Base rates may need to rise to 7.25-7.50 percent over the next year unless fiscal policy is tightened significantly further in the forthcoming budget," he said.
Davies, who is widely expected to be made a deputy governor of the Bank of England by the new government, said raising taxes was not a viable alternative to higher interest rates.
Consumer taxes would need to rise by around nine billion pounds ($14.7 billion) to reduce base rate pressure by one percentage point.
"That seems to us a bit implausible. It doesn't look politically feasible," he added.
The Green Budget was critical of some tax proposals outlined in Labour's manifesto, which may form part of its first budget.
It described the proposed "windfall" tax on the profits of privatised utility firms as an arbitrary measure, difficult to reconcile with any principles of equity in taxation.
However, the study concluded that the windfall tax was unlikely to have much impact on the prices that utility companies charge their customers or on their investment plans.

The two institutions also criticised Labour for toying with the idea of introducing a two-tier capital gains tax -- making investors pay more tax on gains in assets which they hold for only a short time. This would be aimed at encouraging long-term shareholding.
"This proposal is deeply flawed at both the conceptual and the pragmatic levels," the report said.
A two-tier capital gains tax would have almost no impact on shareholders' behaviour as hardly any shareholders in Britain pay the tax, it added.
($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
